title: Converbs II: the more, whenever, because
intro: This unit completes the converbs of B1. `-DIkçA` says **the more** or **whenever**, `-(I)r -mAz` says **as soon as**, and a doubled `-(y)A` (*koşa koşa*) paints the manner of an action; like those of [B1 unit 7](b1-u07-grammar), they take no tense and no person. Two more are built on the `-DIk` participle of [B1 unit 6](gp-participle-dik) and do show the person: `-DIğIndA` for **when**, and `-DIğI için` for **because**.

blocks.text: `-DIkçA` is the participle `-DIk` + `-çA`. Its first vowel follows four-way harmony and its second two-way, and its D becomes t after a voiceless consonant, as in the past: *okudukça*, *geldikçe*, *baktıkça*, *gördükçe*, *gittikçe*. The stem doesn't change: *gittikçe*, *yedikçe*.

**The more … the more.** When the main clause describes a change, `-DIkçA` makes it grow with the first action: *Okudukça seviyorum* (The more I read, the more I like it), *Türkçe konuştukça daha kolay oluyor* (The more you speak Turkish, the easier it gets). *Daha* often marks the change in the main clause.

**Whenever.** With a repeated action, it means **whenever, every time**: *Zaman buldukça kitap okurum* (I read whenever I find the time), *Seni gördükçe annemi hatırlıyorum* (Every time I see you, I think of my mother).
No tense and no person, as in [B1 unit 7](b1-u07-grammar): the main verb gives both, and a different subject is simply named: *Sen konuştukça herkes gülüyor* (Whenever you talk, everyone laughs).

**Two fixed words.** *Gittikçe* (literally **the more it goes**) means **more and more, increasingly**, like *giderek*: *Hava gittikçe ısınıyor* (It's getting warmer and warmer). And *oldukça* (quite, fairly, [A2 unit 8](gp-equative)) began as **the more it is**.

items.en: The more I read, the more I like it.
The more you speak Turkish, the easier it gets.
I read whenever I find the time.

items.tr: Burada yaşadıkça bu şehri daha çok seviyorum.
items.seg: Burada yaşa|dık|ça bu şehri daha çok seviyorum.
items.en: The longer I live here, the more I love this city.
Your Turkish is getting better and better.

blocks.text: `-DIkçA` is not `-(y)IncA`. *Okuyunca* is **when** or **once** you read; *okudukça* is **the more** or **every time** you read.
The negative, `-mAdIkçA`, means something else, **unless**. It comes in [B2 unit 10](gp-madikca).

`-DIğIndA` is the `-DIk` participle of [B1 unit 6](gp-participle-dik) with a possessive ending and the locative `-DA`: *geldiğimde*, literally **at my coming**, means **when I come** or **when I came**. Unlike the converbs so far, it shows the person.

rows.en: when I come, when I came

blocks.text: The third persons add the n of [A1 unit 10](gp-pronominal-n) before the locative: *geldiğinde*, *geldiklerinde*. So **you** and **he** look alike, *geldiğinde*, and a pronoun decides when it matters: *Sen geldiğinde*, *O geldiğinde*. With a plural noun the singular is usual: *Misafirler geldiğinde* (when the guests came).

**Tense** comes from the main verb: *Geldiğinde ararım* (I'll call when you come), *Geldiğimde herkes uyuyordu* (When I got home, everyone was asleep). A named subject usually stays in the nominative, unlike the doer of a relative clause: *Ali geldiğinde* (when Ali came), *Annem aradığında* (when my mother called).

**With nouns and adjectives**, use *olduğumda*: *Hasta olduğumda annem bana çorba yapar* (When I'm ill, my mother makes me soup). For **as a child**, though, `-ken` ([A2 unit 11](gp-ken)) is the usual choice: *çocukken*.
**Every time.** Put *her* in front for **every time**: *seni her gördüğümde* (every time I see you), *İzmir'e her gittiğimde balık yerim* (Every time I go to Izmir, I eat fish).

**-DIğI zaman.** *Geldiğim zaman* means the same as *geldiğimde*, and is just as common: *Geldiğin zaman beni ara* (Call me when you come). It is the participle with *zaman* (time) as its noun, like *tanıştığımız gün* in [B1 unit 6](gp-participle-dik).

**-DIğIndA or -(y)IncA?** Often both work: *Seni görünce sevindim* and *Seni gördüğümde sevindim* (I was glad when I saw you). `-(y)IncA` stresses that one thing followed, or set off, the other. `-DIğIndA` simply places the main event at that time, which suits a background (*Geldiğimde herkes uyuyordu*) and repeated events, and its ending shows the person.

items.en: When I got home, everyone was asleep.
Call me when you get to the hotel.
I wasn't home when my mother called.
Every time I go to Izmir, I eat fish.
When we're on holiday, we don't look at our phones.
Call me when you come.

blocks.text: The k of `-DIk` softens before the vowel of the ending, and stays before *-leri*: *geldiğimde*, *geldiklerinde*. Don't drop it: *geldimde* doesn't exist.

**Because** is the same participle with a possessive ending, followed by *için*: *Hasta olduğum için gelemedim* (I couldn't come because I was ill). The reason comes first. It says what *çünkü* says, in the other order: *Gelemedim, çünkü hastaydım*.

rows.en: because he or she is tired

blocks.text: **No tense of its own.** *Olduğum için* covers **because I am** and **because I was**; the main verb decides. For a future reason, use `-(y)AcAk` in the same pattern: *Yarın erken kalkacağım için şimdi yatıyorum* (I'm going to bed now because I'm getting up early tomorrow).

**Var and yok** become *olduğu* and *olmadığı*: *Sınavım olduğu için çalışıyorum* (I'm studying because I have an exam), *Param olmadığı için gidemiyorum* (I can't go because I have no money). The subject usually stays in the nominative, as with `-DIğIndA`: *Yağmur yağdığı için*, *Hava soğuk olduğu için*.
**-DIğIndAn.** The ablative in place of *için* gives a variant that sounds more written: *Hasta olduğumdan gelemedim*.

**Because of** a noun is *yüzünden*, usually for something bad, and **thanks to** is *sayesinde*. Both are possessed nouns, so their ending follows the owner: *benim yüzümden*, *senin yüzünden*, *onun yüzünden*; *benim sayemde*, *senin sayende*, *onun sayesinde*. After an ordinary noun, use the third person: *trafik yüzünden* (because of the traffic), *bu harita sayesinde* (thanks to this map).
The ablative alone can also give a cause, especially with feelings: *korkudan* (out of fear), *Mutluluktan ağladı* (She cried with happiness).

items.en: I couldn't come because I was ill.
We didn't go out because it was raining.
I can't go on holiday because I have no money.

items.tr: Yarın erken kalkacağım için şimdi yatıyorum.
items.seg: Yarın erken kalk|acağ|ım için şimdi yatıyorum.
items.en: I'm going to bed now because I'm getting up early tomorrow.
I was late for the meeting because of the traffic.
We found the way thanks to you.

blocks.title: Sorry and thank you
blocks.text: Apologies and thanks use this pattern every day: *Geç kaldığım için özür dilerim* (Sorry I'm late), *Yardım ettiğin için teşekkür ederim* (Thank you for helping).

blocks.title: Purpose or reason?
blocks.text: *Görmek için geldim* is **I came to see**: a purpose, looking ahead ([B1 unit 4](gp-purpose)). *Gördüğüm için geldim* is **I came because I saw**: a reason, looking back. Same *için*, different verb form.

Put a verb's aorist next to its negative aorist, both in the plain third person, to say **as soon as**: *Eve gelir gelmez uyudu* (He fell asleep as soon as he got home). The positive comes first, with the aorist vowel of [A2 unit 4](gp-aorist-forms), irregular verbs included: *alır almaz*, *bulur bulmaz*, *görür görmez*.

head: Verb
As soon as…
Example
rows: *Eve gelir gelmez uyudu.* He fell asleep as soon as he got home.
*Mesajı okur okumaz aradım.* I called as soon as I read the message.
*Haberi duyar duymaz geldi.* She came the moment she heard the news.
*Eve varır varmaz ararım.* I'll call as soon as I get home.
*Ders biter bitmez dışarı koştular.* They ran out as soon as the lesson ended.
*Film başlar başlamaz uyudum.* I fell asleep as soon as the film started.

blocks.text: Like the converbs of [B1 unit 7](b1-u07-grammar), it has no person and no tense, and the subjects can differ: *Ben eve varır varmaz yağmur başladı* (It started raining the moment I got home).
It is quicker than `-(y)IncA`: *eve gelince* is **once I'm home**, *eve gelir gelmez* **the very moment I get home**.

items.en: As soon as the bell rang, I opened the door.
I'll call you as soon as I get home.
He ran off the moment he heard the news.

items.tr: Ders biter bitmez öğrenciler dışarı çıktı.
items.seg: Ders bit|er bit|mez öğrenciler dışarı çıktı.
items.en: As soon as the lesson ended, the students went outside.

blocks.title: Olur olmaz
blocks.text: *Olur olmaz* is also an adjective, **any old, every little**: *Olur olmaz şeylere kızıyor* (She gets angry at every little thing).
Only the plain third person: *gelir gelmez*, never *gelirim gelmem*. The main verb says who.

A verb with `-(y)A`, said twice, describes an action that goes on and on, or the manner of the main action: *Koşa koşa geldi* (She came running all the way), *Ağlaya ağlaya anlattı* (She told it in tears). The suffix has two-way harmony and the buffer y after a vowel; *git-* softens and *ye-* writes an i: *gide gide*, *yiye yiye*.
It is livelier than `-(y)ArAk`: *Koşarak geldi* tells you how she came; *Koşa koşa geldi* shows her running. Like `-(y)ArAk`, it belongs to the subject of the main verb.

**Set phrases.** Many doubles are fixed. *Güle güle* (goodbye, said by the one who stays, [A1 unit 1](a1-u01-grammar)) is literally **laughing, laughing**, and *Güle güle kullanın* ([A2 unit 7](gp-set-wishes)) wishes that you use something with joy. *Bile bile* means **knowingly, on purpose**, and *seve seve* **gladly**. The proverb *Damlaya damlaya göl olur* (Drop by drop, a lake forms) is built the same way.

**Two different verbs** can pair up too, for actions that alternate: *düşe kalka* (falling and getting up again): *Bisiklete binmeyi düşe kalka öğrendim* (I learned to ride a bike by falling off and getting back on).

items.en: The children came running home from school.
She told the story in tears.
You did that on purpose!
I'd be glad to help you.
I learned it by reading again and again.

blocks.text: Don't confuse it with the optative `-(y)A` of [A2 unit 7](gp-optative), which takes a person and stands alone: *geleyim*, *gelelim*. Here the bare form comes twice.

summary: `-DIkçA` is **the more** with a change (*Okudukça seviyorum*) and **whenever** with a habit (*Zaman buldukça okurum*); *gittikçe* means **more and more**.
`-DIğIndA` is **when**, with the person: *geldiğimde*, *geldiğinde*, *geldiklerinde*; *her gittiğimde* is **every time I go**, and *geldiğim zaman* means the same as *geldiğimde*.
`-DIğI için` is **because**, with the person, before the result: *Hasta olduğum için gelemedim*; future *kalkacağım için*; *var* becomes *olduğu*.
*Yüzünden* (because of) and *sayesinde* (thanks to) follow the owner: *senin yüzünden*, *senin sayende*, *trafik yüzünden*.
`-(I)r -mAz` is **as soon as**: *gelir gelmez*, *alır almaz*, always in the plain third person.
A doubled `-(y)A` paints an action: *koşa koşa*, *ağlaya ağlaya*; set phrases *güle güle*, *bile bile*, *seve seve*.
The subject of these time and reason clauses usually stays in the nominative: *Ali geldiğinde*, *Hava soğuk olduğu için*.
